title: Is it a sin to drink, get a tattoo, or gamble?
seoTitle: Is It a Sin to Drink, Get a Tattoo, or Gamble?
description: Is drinking, a tattoo, or gambling a sin? What the Bible forbids, what it leaves to conscience, Romans 14 and Leviticus 19:28 in context, and how to decide.
summary: What Scripture forbids, what it leaves to conscience, and how to decide the rest without pride or fear.
askedAs: is it a sin to get a tattoo
is playing the lottery a sin
is it a sin to swear
answer: You want to know whether a drink, a tattoo, or a bet would be a sin, and you'd like a straight answer. Maybe you grew up with a list of rules and can't tell anymore which ones were God's, or someone you love draws the line somewhere else. Scripture is plain where it speaks plainly: drunkenness is sin, and so is greed. On much of the rest it does something harder than hand you a rule. It marks out room where faithful Christians decide differently before God, and it shows how to decide there: with a clear conscience, with thanks, without letting anything master you, and with love for the person beside you. If drinking or gambling already has a hold on you, the question has changed; start with [our page on addiction](/help/addiction). If you're in recovery, nothing on this page asks you to find out whether you can handle it now.
happening:
The question usually comes with a story attached. You may have grown up where Christians didn't drink, play cards, or get tattoos, and now you're holding a glass of wine with a feeling you can't quite name. Or you came to faith later and were handed a list, or nothing at all. Maybe you married into a family that toasts every holiday, and your own father drank the rent money. Maybe your daughter wants a tattoo, your friends bet on every game from their phones, or a believer you respect does what you were taught never to do. And sometimes, if we're honest, we ask hoping for a particular answer, because we've already decided.

The two common answers each get something right. Many churches say *good Christians just don't*, and that's partly true: holiness is real, and some of these things have wrecked real lives. But Scripture refuses to turn some matters into rules, and it has hard words for people who add rules of their own. The culture around us says *it's your life, so do what seems right to you*, and that's partly true too, since Scripture does leave real matters to conscience and rules people make up can't make anyone holy. What that answer misses is that God does forbid some things, and that Christian freedom always has a neighbor in view.

Underneath both is your conscience, formed by your parents, your church, and your past. It matters. Paul says that acting against it is sin, even when the act itself is permitted (Romans 14:23). But it isn't infallible either. "My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me," he told the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 4:4). Feeling guilty doesn't prove you sinned, and feeling fine doesn't prove you didn't.

Both answers also miss that Scripture sorts these questions three ways, not two. Some things God commands, some he forbids, and some he leaves to each believer to settle before him, where "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5). Careful Christians don't always agree which questions belong there (drinking at all, tattoos, and gambling among them), so hold your own answer humbly. In that third space, *Am I allowed?* is only the first question, and rarely the hardest.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't settle every gray-area question with a verse, but it shows how to think about them. Jesus starts with the heart. Paul writes to churches in Rome, Corinth, and Galatia that were divided over food, holy days, and the law of Moses, and shows how love should govern them.

passages.text: You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men. ... Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him. ... For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.
passages.reading: Pharisees and scribes challenged Jesus because his disciples ate without the ceremonial hand-washing their tradition required (Mark 7:1-5). He answered that they had set God's command aside to keep their own rules, and gave an example: their tradition let a man declare his support for his parents a gift devoted to God, and then forbade him to help them (Mark 7:11-12). A religious rule had become a way around love. Then Jesus moved defilement from the plate to the heart, and Mark adds, "Thus all foods are clean" (Mark 7:19). But read the list that follows: greed, debauchery, slander, and envy are on it. Holiness now lives in the one place no rule can reach, and it asks more of us there.

passages.text: Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions. ... The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him. ... I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean. ... But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.
passages.reading: Paul wrote to a church in Rome he had not yet visited (Romans 1:13), divided over food and holy days. He agrees with the strong that nothing is unclean in itself, and counts himself among them (Romans 15:1), but he spends most of the chapter restraining them. Freedom gives no one the right to look down on the careful, and caution gives no one the right to condemn the free, because God has accepted both. Then comes the line that protects every conscience (Romans 14:23): no one may be bullied into freedom, any more than shamed out of it. A few verses earlier the same letter names "carousing and drunkenness" among the deeds of darkness (Romans 13:13), so the chapter guards the room God left open inside walls he has already built.

passages.text: Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.
passages.reading: Some believers in Corinth knew that an idol is nothing (1 Corinthians 8:4) and concluded they could eat anywhere, even in a temple's dining room. Paul grants their theology and questions their love: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1). The weak brother here isn't someone who merely disapproves of you. He's a believer with a weak conscience who might follow your example into what that conscience calls idolatry, and be ruined by it. Today he might be a new believer who can't yet separate a glass of wine from the life he left, and the same love reaches a friend fighting to stay sober. Paul limits himself rather than making a rule for everyone, and two chapters later he won't let someone else's conscience become the measure of his own (1 Corinthians 10:29). He also makes clear that a meal at an idol's own table was never a gray area (1 Corinthians 10:20-21).

passages.text: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery. ... For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love. The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
passages.reading: Paul wrote to churches in Galatia where teachers were pressing Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, as though Christ were not enough (Galatians 5:2-4 and 6:12). He resists that yoke with everything he has. Then, in the same chapter, he faces the opposite danger: freedom is not "an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13), and a few lines later drunkenness appears among the acts of the flesh (Galatians 5:21). One apostle names both traps on one page. Having warned against a yoke of slavery, Paul tells free people to serve one another in love, quoting Leviticus 19:18, from the same chapter that holds the verse about tattoos. Christ frees us from a yoke so that we can carry each other.

whyHard:
The usual explanation for all this confusion is that the Bible is unclear or the churches are inconsistent, and there's truth in both. Scripture says nothing about vapes or betting apps, and churches do draw their lines in different places. But the deeper trouble is in us. We tend to want a rule more than we want wisdom. A rule tells you exactly where the line is, lets you stand right next to it, and gives you a way to measure everyone else. Wisdom keeps asking what a thing is doing to you and to the person beside you, and it never stops asking.

The church has argued about such things since its first generation. Christians have long called them adiaphora, a Greek word for *things indifferent*. The phrase doesn't mean they're unimportant; it means God neither commands nor forbids them. Paul's own practice shows how they work. He circumcised Timothy "on account of the Jews in that area" (Acts 16:3), setting freedom aside so the gospel would get a hearing. But when false brothers wanted Titus circumcised, he wrote, "We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you" (Galatians 2:5). The same act was love in one case and surrender in the other. Freedom bends for a brother. It does not bow to anyone who says Christ isn't enough.

For most of its history the church used wine at the Lord's Table. In 1869 a New Jersey dentist named Thomas Welch began pasteurizing grape juice so his church could take communion without alcohol, and over time many American churches made the same change. The temperance movement drew Christians who had seen what drink did to families, and it helped carry the country into Prohibition, from 1920 until 1933. If you abstain, you can read that history as love: a church that watched drink ruin homes and gave up wine for the sake of the weak, as Paul commends in Romans 14:21. If you drink, you can read a warning in it: a conviction born in love can harden into a test of fellowship the New Testament never set. Both readings see something true, and whichever tradition raised you probably feels like the plain meaning of the Bible.

Underneath, the legalist and the libertine have more in common than either would like. Both keep the self at the center. One uses rules to secure his standing and keep score on others; the other uses freedom to secure his comfort and keep others quiet. Neither trap belongs to one camp. A drinker can keep score as fiercely as any legalist, and a lifelong abstainer can still be ruled by appetite somewhere else, and the letter to the Colossians says as much: rules about food and drink "have an appearance of wisdom" but "are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). Both traps make Christ smaller than he is.

I came to faith from atheism, so I understand why a skeptic might watch Christians argue over tattoos and card games and decide the faith is a dress code. The New Testament is less impressed by dress codes than the skeptic expects. And those of us who preach are inside this. We've been tempted to hand people a list because lists are easy to preach, and tempted to say nothing because we didn't want to sound strict while someone's freedom was quietly taking their marriage apart. Christ bought our freedom with his own life. It was meant to be given away.

thisWeek.intro: You don't need to settle every gray area this week. Start with the one in front of you, and go slowly enough to hear both Scripture and the people your choice will touch. The first step takes five minutes.

steps.title: Write down why you're asking
steps.body: Put the question on paper, *Is it wrong for me to drink?* or *Should I get this tattoo?*, and under it write why you're asking. Do you want permission? Do you want someone else to stop? Are you afraid something already has a grip on you? The reason often tells you more than the rule does.

steps.title: Read Paul, then ask his questions
steps.body: Read 1 Corinthians 8 to 10 in one sitting, so no verse gets lifted out of its place. Paul gave the Corinthians questions that still work. Does it build others up (1 Corinthians 10:23)? Will it master me? When some in Corinth excused their appetites with "Everything is permissible for me," Paul answered, "but I will not be mastered by anything" (1 Corinthians 6:12). Can I do it with thanks, to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31)? Will it lead someone to act against their own conscience (1 Corinthians 8:9)? If you can't answer honestly, ask someone who knows you well.

steps.title: Put some time between you and it
steps.body: Set the habit aside for thirty days and notice what happens in you, but if you've been drinking heavily every day, talk to a doctor before you stop, because withdrawal can be dangerous. It might be the drink at night, the lottery ticket, or the betting app. If that's easy, you've learned something good; if it's hard, you've learned something important. If you're in recovery, skip this test, because staying away is how you keep your freedom. Something permanent, like a tattoo, deserves a season of prayer and counsel before you decide.

steps.title: Talk with the people it touches
steps.body: Your freedom has neighbors. If you're married, your spouse belongs in this decision, and your histories will tell you more than trading verses: a spouse who grew up with a parent's drinking isn't being legalistic when they ask you to bend, and a spouse who asks for room isn't being worldly. If you're young and live at home, your parents' answer carries weight (Ephesians 6:1). If a friend at church abstains, ask what it means to them, and decide what you'll do in their company. Paul's aim was "what leads to peace and to mutual edification" (Romans 14:19).

steps.title: Make peace with the other side
steps.body: If you've looked down on a believer for being strict, or judged one for being free, go and say so, in person if you can. Romans 14:3 forbids both, because God has accepted both. You can keep your conviction and still repent of your contempt.

moreHelp.body:
Most of these questions belong to prayer, Scripture, and honest friends. Some don't. When drinking or gambling has a grip you can't break, the question is no longer whether it's allowed. Start with [our page on addiction](/help/addiction) and your doctor. SAMHSA's helpline, listed with the other help lines at the end of this page, can point you to treatment for drinking or drug use. For gambling, ask your doctor or a licensed counselor for someone who treats gambling problems, and if it has left you in debt, see [our page on money](/help/money).

Conscience itself can become a torment. If you're asking whether more and more ordinary things are sins, confessing the same act again and again, or needing reassurance that never lasts, that fear deserves real care, and needing care is no failure of faith. To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, search your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which local counselors they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about license and training as well as faith, and check the license with your state.
signs: You've tried to cut back on drinking and can't, or you need a drink to get through the day. If you drink heavily every day, see a doctor before you stop.
You bet to win back losses, hide how much you've spent, or borrow to keep playing.
Drinking or gambling has put your rent, your bills, or your family's needs at risk.
You or someone you love drives after drinking. Take the keys if you safely can, and call 911 if someone is in danger on the road.
Fear that ordinary things are sins keeps you checking, confessing, or seeking reassurance, and the relief never lasts.
You've had thoughts of ending your life, over drinking, debt, or anything else. Call or text 988 now.
moreHelp.firstCall: Plain words are enough. To a doctor: *I'm drinking more than I want to, and I can't cut back.* To a counselor: *I've been gambling more than I can afford, and I'm hiding it,* or *I'm afraid all the time that I'm sinning, and nothing settles it.* Ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they treat this problem, what it costs, and whether they take your insurance. If your faith matters to you, say so, and ask how they work with Christian clients.
moreHelp.cost: Many counselors offer sliding-scale fees, and community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less. An employee assistance program may include a few free sessions. SAMHSA's helpline can point you to state-funded treatment for drinking or drug use, nonprofit credit counseling for debt is often free or low-cost, and your church may have a benevolence fund.

helping.body:
If someone brings you this question, find out what's behind it before you answer. A teenager asking about tattoos, a new believer asking about wine, and a friend asking about gambling while hiding what they've lost are asking three different questions.

Answer honestly, including where Christians disagree. Parents are tempted to present a house rule as a commandment, or to say nothing at all, and children notice both. You can say, *In our house we don't, and here's why,* without claiming God said it. As the father of five sons, I would rather they hear from me which rules are mine and which are God's than discover it on their own. Pastors owe their people the same clarity about which of the church's expectations come from Scripture and which are wisdom or policy.

And if the person you're helping can't stop, set the theology aside for now. They need help finding help.
say: What's behind the question for you?
Here's what Scripture says plainly, and here's where it leaves room.
Christians I respect land in different places on this one.
I've noticed it's been harder for you to stop. Can we talk about it?
Whatever you decide, it won't change how I see you.
dontSay: The Bible doesn't mention it, so it's fine.
If you really loved Jesus, you wouldn't want to.
helping.next: Offer to read Romans 14 together, slowly, and keep talking after either of you decides. If drinking or gambling has a grip, help them call a doctor or a counselor this week, offer a ride, and keep checking in. If they speak of ending their life, stay with them and call or text 988 together.

prayer:
Lord, I want to know where your lines are, and I confess I sometimes want to know so I can stand right next to them. "Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns" (Psalm 139:23).

Forgive me for looking down on a brother for being careful, and for judging a sister for being free. Forgive me for calling it freedom when it was only appetite, and holiness when it was only fear.

Where you've spoken plainly, make me obey. Where you've left me free, make me grateful, and quick to set my freedom down for someone who needs me to. If something has begun to master me, give me the courage to say so to someone who can help.

Your Son was free as no one has ever been free, and he spent his freedom on a cross. Make me free like that. Amen.

faq.a: Scripture plainly forbids drunkenness: "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion" (Ephesians 5:18). Whether to drink at all is where faithful Christians differ. Those who drink in moderation note that a psalm praises "wine that gladdens the heart of man" (Psalm 104:15), that the law let Israel spend its tithe money on wine at the feast (Deuteronomy 14:26), and that Jesus made wine at a wedding in Cana (John 2:1-11). They receive it as a gift, with thanks. Those who abstain note that Scripture honors people who refused wine, like the Nazirites (Numbers 6:3) and the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35), that Proverbs warns it "bites like a snake" (Proverbs 23:32), and that Paul wrote, "It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble" (Romans 14:21). They set it down for love of the neighbor who can't stop. If you're under the legal drinking age, the law has already answered. If you're in recovery, staying away is wisdom, not legalism, and no one should press a drink on you. If you can't stop, start with [our page on addiction](/help/addiction) and a doctor.

faq.q: Is it a sin to get a tattoo?
faq.a: The verse people cite is Leviticus 19:28: "You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead or put tattoo marks on yourselves. I am the LORD." It stands in a chapter that commands love of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) and forbids mixing two kinds of fabric (Leviticus 19:19) and trimming the edges of the beard (Leviticus 19:27), and it pairs the marks with cutting the body for the dead, a mourning rite Deuteronomy also forbids (Deuteronomy 14:1). Christians read it two ways. Some place it with the beard and fabric laws, as one of the marks that set Israel apart from the nations, never repeated in the New Testament; for them a tattoo is a matter of freedom and wisdom. Others note that the same chapter's bans on theft and on consulting mediums still bind (Leviticus 19:11, 31), and that God still cares how his people mark the bodies they're told to offer him (Romans 12:1); for them it remains a line God drew. If you're young and live at home, your parents' answer carries weight. On either reading, your standing with God rests on Christ, not your skin.

Scripture never names gambling, and when it describes casting lots it's usually a way of leaving a decision to God (Proverbs 16:33), not a wager. So Christians reason from principles and land in different places. Some hold that gambling is wrong in itself: it feeds the wish to get rich, and 1 Timothy warns that those who want to be rich fall into desires that "plunge them into ruin and destruction" (1 Timothy 6:9); it seeks gain from a neighbor's loss rather than from work (Ephesians 4:28); and they want no part in an industry that profits from people who can't stop. Others hold that a small bet among friends, a raffle, or a lottery ticket bought for fun is spending on entertainment, no different in principle from a ballgame ticket, and that making a rule of it goes beyond Scripture (Colossians 2:20-23); kept small, it's a freedom to enjoy with thanks. Both agree on the hard lines: betting money your household needs is wrong (1 Timothy 5:8), and chasing losses, hiding them, or borrowing to play are signs of a grip that needs help, not a debate. Start with [our page on addiction](/help/addiction).

faq.q: Is it a sin to swear or cuss?
faq.a: It depends on what you mean, because Scripture speaks to three things. When Jesus tells his hearers "not to swear at all" (Matthew 5:34), he means oaths, calling on heaven or earth to back your word, and his point is honesty: "Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’" (Matthew 5:37). The Ten Commandments forbid taking "the name of the LORD your God in vain" (Exodus 20:7), which includes using his name as a curse. And Scripture speaks to crude and cruel words: "Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths" (Ephesians 4:29). Some Christians hold that certain words are off-limits in themselves, citing the same letter's warning against "obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking" (Ephesians 5:4). Others hold that which words count as crude shifts with time and place, so the test is the one Ephesians 4:29 goes on to give: whether speech builds up the one who hears it. Both agree that words meant to wound or demean are wrong, because "out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34).

faq.q: Is smoking or vaping a sin?
faq.a: Scripture never mentions tobacco, so Christians reason from principles. The line people often quote, "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:19), comes from Paul's warning against sexual immorality, though its point, that your body isn't your own, reaches further, and Paul also urges believers to offer their bodies to God "as living sacrifices" (Romans 12:1). Smoking harms nearly every organ of the body, and nicotine, smoked or vaped, is highly addictive. Some Christians conclude that taking up something so harmful and habit-forming is poor care of a body God made and will raise. Others treat it as a matter of freedom and wisdom, like what we eat, while urging caution. Both would say that being mastered by it is a real danger (1 Corinthians 6:12), and that smoke around children is a question of love. If you're under the legal age, the law has answered for you.

slots.note: Where James lands on drinking, moderation or abstinence, in his own words, and, if he wishes, the tradition his view comes from. The answer to 'Is drinking alcohol a sin?' gives each view its texts and its comfort and deliberately does not land, and the temperance paragraph of Why this is so hard reads that history both ways. The addiction page carries the same slot, so one statement from James could serve both pages.

Where James lands on tattoos, and how he reads Leviticus 19:28: with the beard and fabric laws as a mark of Israel's separation, or as still speaking to how believers mark their bodies. The FAQ answer states both readings and does not land.

Where James lands on gambling: a lottery ticket, an office pool, a church raffle, a sports-betting app. The answer states the view that gambling is wrong in itself and the view that small stakes spent as entertainment are permitted, gives each its texts, and does not land.

If James wants to, a sentence on where he lands on swearing (whether some words are wrong in themselves or wrong by what they do) and on smoking and vaping. Both answers state the views and say only what both sides share.

The page says only that James came to faith from atheism and so understands why a skeptic might take the faith for a dress code. He could add, in his own words, how the church's rules about drinking, cards, or tattoos looked to him from outside, or how he sorted Scripture's lines from a church's after he believed. Only from James; the paragraph stands without it.

The page states only James's conviction as a father of five sons, that he would rather they hear from him which rules are his and which are God's. He could add, in his own words, how he talks with his sons about drinking, tattoos, or gambling. No story has been written for him.

Every passage setting rechecked with scripts/bsb.mjs --verses (Mark 7:1-23; Romans 1:13, 12:1, 13:11-15:3; 1 Corinthians 4:3-5, 6:12-20, 8, 9:19-22, 10:14-33; Galatians 2:1-5, 5, 6:12-13; Acts 16:1-4; Colossians 2:16-23; Leviticus 19:9-37; Deuteronomy 14:1-2, 24-26; Numbers 6:3, 20; Jeremiah 35; Proverbs 16:33, 23:29-32; John 19:23-24; Matthew 5:33-37, 12:34; Exodus 20:7; Ephesians 4:28-29, 5:3-4, 5:18, 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:8, 6:9-10; Psalm 104:14-15, 139:23). Fixed: the gambling answer said Scripture never describes lots as a wager, but the soldiers cast lots for Jesus' tunic to see who would get it (John 19:24), so it now says usually; the Colossian opponents are described by what 2:16 and 2:21 name (rules about food and drink), not as adding food laws; works of the flesh now follows the BSB's acts; the Scripture intro no longer says Rome was divided over wine; the Galatian demand is glossed from 5:4 (as though Christ were not enough), not in order to belong. 1 Corinthians 8 in context: the weak brother is weak in conscience, not willpower (8:7, 10, 12), so the reading no longer makes a friend fighting to stay sober the nearest modern case; it names a new believer whose conscience ties wine to the life he left and extends the same love to the friend in recovery. Kept, as well established and stated no more strongly than that: wine at the Lord's Table for most of church history, Welch's grape juice for communion in 1869, the temperance movement's part in Prohibition (1920 to 1933), smoking harms nearly every organ. Sources: the uncertain CDC vaping address dropped; the page now says only that nicotine, smoked or vaped, is highly addictive, not that most vapes contain it; the withdrawal claim now says drinking heavily every day, matching the page. Tilt: the drinking FAQ opened by saying Scripture forbids drunkenness, not wine, a landing before either side spoke; it now says Scripture plainly forbids drunkenness and that whether to drink at all is where faithful Christians differ. The smoking FAQ no longer tells one side its verse should not be stretched (it gives 1 Corinthians 6:19 its context and its reach) and calls mastery a real danger, not the real one. The permissive view of gambling now has its comfort, and the second view of swearing its verse (the test of Ephesians 4:29). The spouse counsel asked only the freer spouse to bend; both now get their due. Parents are warned against saying nothing as well as against passing off a house rule as God's. The legalist and the libertine now belong to neither camp, with Colossians 2:23 cutting both ways.
